attribution: Presented as the teaching of Shiva; author unknown
period: Scholars place it between roughly the 15th and 17th centuries CE; dating is debated
summary: A hatha yoga text that joins subtle-body practice with a broadly Vedantic, non-dual view of the self.
whyRead: It is notable for grounding hatha practice in a metaphysical frame close to Advaita, and for describing the subtle body in detail. It also states that householders can practise yoga successfully.
questions: Can bodily yoga be joined to a non-dual philosophy?

keyTeachings.title: A philosophical opening
keyTeachings.text: The first chapter surveys competing views and then favours a non-dual position in which the individual self is not ultimately different from the supreme. The practical chapters are set within this frame.

keyTeachings.title: The body as microcosm
keyTeachings.text: The body is described as containing the cosmos in miniature, with channels (nadi), centres and the central channel, through which the practice is mapped.

keyTeachings.title: Practice for householders
keyTeachings.text: The text holds that success in yoga depends on practice rather than on renouncing household life, a point often cited in discussions of who yoga is for.
